rationale: A wins because it keeps the story inside the facts and turns one announcement into four clean reporter doors: P&L, moat strategy, driver cost, and connector infrastructure. "An unprofitable automaker just turned its charging network into a revenue line" is a real markets angle with the missing proof named instead of wallpapered over. B keeps reaching for a bigger movie than the update supports, especially "After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs" and "Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet." That is how an angle set gets dressed up for an editor and then dies in fact-check.
gaps_in_A: "The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat" is a useful thesis, but it is not in the supplied facts. A flags the proof need, so this is a bruise, not a fracture.
"with no automaker partnership to force its hand" leans harder than the facts allow. The update says no partnership was announced; it does not prove no commercial pressure or negotiation existed.
The set gives four viable routes but does not rank the strongest first. For a founder, the pricing delta and utilization baseline probably decide whether the revenue angle deserves priority.
gaps_in_B: "After Tesla, Rivian opens its charging network to all EVs" smuggles in an outside news peg. The supplied update says Tesla-style NACS connectors, not Tesla's Supercharger strategy.
"The proprietary-charger era is fading" is a trend claim wearing a trench coat. One Rivian announcement plus an imported Tesla comparison is not enough evidence.
"Rivian just became a charging-network operator. Wall Street hasn't repriced it yet." Rivian already operated the Adventure Network, and the repricing claim invents market reaction not in the facts.
Angle 1 and angle 4 are padded cousins: "financial-strategy story" versus "investment thesis" both need the same missing materiality proof before a reporter cares.
